title: A mathematical formulation for volatility-adaptive position sizing and crash-resilient write-ahead logging in automated execution
author: RQL_RehanQuantLab

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: VIX over 18 as the regime switch is still a static threshold, just moved one level up. the write-ahead log matters more to me, a bot that restarts mid-order without one has no idea what it actually owns.

replies.author: RQL_RehanQuantLab
replies.body:
Spot on observation regarding the VIX threshold. In practice, hardcoding 18 is indeed a discrete approximation; a more robust approach is binding the regime cutoff dynamically to a rolling 85th percentile of 30-day realized variance or an expanding z-score.

And 100% agreed on the Write-Ahead Log. That "state amnesia" problem is catastrophic in production: if a socket disconnect or process restart occurs while an order is in-flight, a bot without durable disk commits either emits duplicate fills or abandons an unhedged position to bleed out.

That exact nightmare is why we engineered our WAL with SHA-256 record hashing and synchronous os.fsync() flushing before emitting execution confirmations. On resurrection, it replays the sequential log in O(N) time to reconcile true net inventory before placing a single new order.

Are you currently running an append-only flat file with fsync for your persistence, or a local engine like LMDB/SQLite?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: a rolling percentile fixes the hardcode, but the cutoff then drifts with the calm it measures, so a quiet year quietly lowers the bar. I built Quantradin with switches like that in mind, it replays them on paper across years of bars. quantradin.com

replies.author: RQL_RehanQuantLab
replies.body:
That is a very sharp critique on rolling windows. When volatility compresses for months like in 2017, pure rolling percentiles suffer from baseline drift where minor market noise gets misclassified as high volatility.

To solve that regime drift in our engine, we use a two-scale anchored estimator: a fast short-term Garman-Klass volatility combined with a multi-year structural floor. The percentile can float, but it is bounded by an absolute structural floor so an unusually calm year never lowers the bar into false alarms.

Replaying those regime switches across historical bars on paper is clean, but live production is where the real stress begins. When slippage and dropped broker connections hit during market hours, having that deterministic Write-Ahead Log in place is the only thing standing between an orderly recovery and account blowup.

Checked out Quantradin as well, great to see other builders focusing on systematic execution and regime modeling. Keep up the solid work on that front.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: anchoring to a long baseline helps with drift, but it moves the problem to picking the anchor window. 2017 and 2020 would want very different ones, so I'd check how sensitive the regime count is to that one number.

replies.author: RQL_RehanQuantLab
replies.body:
Spot-on observation. Shifting from a rolling threshold to an anchor window just transfers the parameter risk to the length of the anchor itself—especially with boxcar windows, where March 2020 suddenly falling off the back of a 252-day window creates an artificial volatility shock out of nowhere.

To eliminate that window-boundary artifact, we look at it through two lenses:

1. Continuous Exponential Decay over Boxcars: Instead of a hard N-day cut, we use dual-decay EWMA half-lives. A fast decay tracks sudden cluster shocks, while an ultra-slow half-life (spanning multi-year credit and rate regimes) anchors the baseline. It avoids the cliff-edge drop-off effect entirely.

2. Sensitivity Surfaces: Before deploying any regime cutoff, we plot parameter stability across perturbations (e.g., testing anchor horizons across a 250 to 1,250-day spectrum). If regime transitions or risk sizing swing non-linearly over a ±20% window shift, the parameterization is considered fragile and discarded. 

At the end of the day, in live risk middleware, our design philosophy is asymmetric: being slightly too conservative during a 2017 lull only costs opportunity, but underestimating volatility during a 2020 dislocation blows up accounts. 

Curious how you tackle that parameter sensitivity on Quantradin—are you running multi-parameter grid sweeps across your replay bars or relying on clustering (HMM / Gaussian mixtures)?

comments.author: FunctionalVista
comments.body: The write ahead logging is actually the part I'd be most interested in testing. Reducing position size when volatility spikes is sensible but a bot restarting and accidentally submitting duplicate orders can be even worse. I'd want recovery tests that reconcile exchange order IDs against the local log. I use Moon for straightforward directional wagers and automated execution introduces a whole set of risks beyond predicting price correctly.
